subsection: 8. Case study: the Jarrow March, October 1936

notes.b: Jarrow was a shipbuilding town on the south bank of the River Tyne whose economy depended on a single employer, and its collapse in the early 1930s left most of its people without work.
points: Jarrow lay on the south bank of the Tyne in County Durham, and its main employer was Palmers Shipbuilding and Iron Company, whose yard had built ships since the nineteenth century.
Palmers and the town's steelworks had been the basis of its employment, and by the early 1930s unemployment in Jarrow was among the highest in Britain.
The shipbuilding industry declined through the 1920s and 1930s because of falling world trade, the lack of new orders and competition from other shipbuilding nations.
The National Shipbuilders Security company, formed in 1930, bought up and closed redundant shipyards on the Tyne, Wear and Clyde in order to reduce the capacity of the industry.
Palmers' yard closed in 1934 after the company was taken over and its shipbuilding activity ended, leaving thousands of men in the town without any work.
The closure left Jarrow with almost no alternative employment, and the town became the symbol of the distressed areas of the north-east.

notes.h: Organising the march, September to October 1936
notes.b: The Jarrow Crusade was organised by the town's council and its Labour MP, who sought a government response to unemployment in the town.
points: Ellen Wilkinson, the Labour MP for Jarrow from 1935, and the town council organised a campaign to press the government for new industries in the town.
The Jarrow Crusade brought together unemployed men, councillors and local clergy in a campaign of petitions, meetings and lobbying of ministers in London.
The marchers numbered about 200 men, selected from the unemployed of the town, and were supported by local churches, trade unions and charities.

The marchers were supported by the local authority, which paid for their travel and expenses, although the national leaders of the Labour Party and the Trades Union Congress were cautious about endorsing the march.
The organisers hoped that a visible protest would force the government to take action in the same way that the earlier hunger marches had drawn attention to unemployment.
The marchers left Jarrow on 5 October 1936 carrying a petition on behalf of the town and marched south towards London.

notes.h: The march and its reception, 5-31 October 1936
notes.b: The march took almost four weeks to reach London, and along the route it attracted large crowds, public sympathy and some practical help.
points: The marchers walked about 300 miles from Jarrow to London, arriving on 31 October 1936, and the route passed through the north of England and the Midlands.
Local people in towns along the route offered food, lodging and money, and the marchers were welcomed by crowds in several places.
The march was reported widely in the national press, and newsreels showed the marchers arriving in London.
In London the marchers presented the petition to the House of Commons, and Ellen Wilkinson spoke for them in the Commons debate.
The Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, refused to meet the marchers, and the government's response was limited to a statement that it was already helping the town.
The marchers were received in London by local political figures and supporters, and they went home by train after their arrival rather than continuing the protest.

notes.h: Outcomes: the return home and the government's response
notes.b: The march brought limited practical results, with the government's policies for the distressed areas expanded only slowly.
points: The government did not offer the new industry that the marchers had asked for, and Baldwin's refusal to meet them was widely criticised in the press.
After the march, unemployment benefit payments were cut for some unemployed men in the north-east, a result that the marchers opposed.
The Special Areas (Amendment) Act of 1937 gave the depressed areas more money for new industries and public works than the 1934 Act had done.
Rearmament from 1937 and 1938 brought new orders to Tyneside shipyards, and unemployment in the north-east fell sharply by 1939.
Ellen Wilkinson's book The Town That Was Murdered, published in 1939, described the closure and its effect on the people of Jarrow.
The march became a lasting symbol of the struggle against unemployment, and later accounts have presented it as a moment of national protest.

notes.b: Contemporaries and later historians disagree about whether the march was a success or a failure, depending on whether they judge it by its immediate aims or by its wider effects.
points: Supporters of the march saw it as an important demonstration of unity and dignity among the unemployed, and a protest against the neglect of the north-east.
Critics in the government and the press argued that the march was a publicity stunt and that the problems of Jarrow could not be solved by government action alone.
The Labour Party's national leadership and the Trades Union Congress were ambivalent, because they feared that the march would be used to attack their own policies.
Later historians have stressed that the march shows the limits of local protest, because Jarrow's economy could only be rebuilt through national investment and rearmament.
Some historians have argued that the march drew attention to the regional problems of the 1930s and helped build support for the Special Areas legislation.
The Jarrow Crusade is remembered as a symbol of working-class protest, and its anniversary has been marked in the town for decades.

notes.b: Judgements of the march depend on whether it is measured by the government's response in 1936 or by the wider impact on policy and public memory.
points: Achievement: the march drew national attention to the plight of Jarrow and the distressed areas, and it helped keep regional unemployment on the political agenda.
Limit: the government refused to meet the marchers, and no new industry was secured for the town in 1936.
Achievement: the march contributed to the Special Areas (Amendment) Act of 1937, which increased government support for the depressed regions.
Limit: the rearmament boom, rather than the march itself, was the main cause of the recovery in Jarrow and on Tyneside after 1937.
Contemporary view: many Conservatives regarded the march as an attempt to exploit the unemployed for political ends.
Later view: historians generally see the march as a moment of protest that failed in its immediate aims but later shaped the memory of the 1930s.
